topic: Compose performance: stability, keys & lazy lists

questions.question: Without strong skipping, when can Compose skip calling a child composable while its parent recomposes?
options: When all its parameters are stable and unchanged
When all of its parameters have default values
When it is annotated with `@Preview`
When it is declared `private`
questions.explanation: Compose skips a composable only if every parameter is of a stable type and compares equal to what was passed last time. Default values, visibility and preview annotations have nothing to do with skipping.

questions.question: How does the Compose compiler infer the stability of this class?
options: Unstable, because it has a public `var`
Stable, because data classes generate `equals()`
Stable, because `String` and `Int` are both stable types
It is a compile error to pass a data class with a `var` to a composable
questions.explanation: A public mutable property that isn't backed by snapshot state makes the class unstable: it can be mutated behind Compose's back. Having `equals()` and stable property types isn't enough once a property is a plain `var`.

questions.question: Sorting a 5,000-item list directly in a composable body (e.g. `val sorted = items.sortedBy { it.name }`) is fine, because a composable body only runs once.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A composable body can run again on every recomposition, sometimes every frame during animations. Wrap it in `remember(items) { ... }` or, better, compute it in the ViewModel.

questions.question: Under strong skipping, unstable parameters like `List` are compared with `===`. What does this print?
questions.code:
data class Item(val id: Int)

fun main() {
    val a = listOf(Item(1), Item(2))
    val b = a.toList()
    val c = a
    println("${a == b} ${a === b} ${a === c}")
}
options: true false true
true true true
false false true
true false false
questions.explanation: `toList()` makes a new list with the same elements, so `==` (structural) is `true` but `===` (identity) is `false`. `c` is the same reference as `a`, so `a === c` is `true`.

questions.question: Why pass `key = { it.id }` to `items(...)` in a `LazyColumn`?
options: So item state follows the item when the list is reordered or changed
So the list is sorted by `id`
So `LazyColumn` composes every item up front instead of lazily
Because `items` doesn't compile without a key
questions.explanation: Without keys, items are identified by position, so inserting at the top shifts remembered state to the wrong rows and recomposes everything after it. A stable key ties state (and item animations) to the item itself; keys are optional and don't sort anything.

questions.question: Which parameter types does the Compose compiler treat as stable on its own (no strong skipping, no stability config)?
options: `Int`
`String`
`(Int) -> Unit`
`@Immutable data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)`
`List<String>`
`data class Form(var email: String)`
questions.explanation: Primitives, `String`, function types and classes with only stable `val`s (or marked `@Immutable`/`@Stable`) are stable. `List` is an interface whose implementation might be mutable, so it's unstable, and a `var` property makes `Form` unstable.

questions.question: What happens when this screen is shown?
options: It crashes, because a `LazyColumn` is measured with infinite max height
It works, but the `LazyColumn` composes every item at once
Only the `LazyColumn` scrolls and the header stays fixed
The two scroll containers share scrolling automatically with no issues
questions.explanation: `verticalScroll` gives its children unbounded height, and a `LazyColumn` can't be measured with infinite height, so Compose throws. Put the header inside the `LazyColumn` as an `item { }` instead.

questions.question: You want to show a "scroll to top" button once the first item has scrolled off. Which is the right way to compute `show`?
options: `val show by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }`
`val show = remember { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 }`
`val show = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex` compared in a `LaunchedEffect(Unit)` that runs once
`val show = rememberSaveable { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 }`
questions.explanation: `derivedStateOf` reads the fast-changing index but only triggers recomposition when the boolean result flips. A plain `remember { ... }` (or `rememberSaveable`) computes it once and never updates, and a one-shot `LaunchedEffect` also never re-checks.

questions.question: This is why a mutated `var` can leave Compose showing stale UI. What does this print?
questions.code:
data class Cart(var count: Int)

fun main() {
    val cart = Cart(1)
    val previous = cart
    cart.count = 2
    println(previous == cart)
    println(previous.count)
}
options:
true
2

false
2

true
1

false
1
questions.explanation: `previous` and `cart` are the same object, so after `cart.count = 2` both see `2` and they compare equal. If Compose compared old and new parameters here, it would see "no change" and skip, even though the data did change.

questions.question: `scroll` is a `ScrollState`. Why is the second version better while the user scrolls?
options: The lambda reads `scroll.value` in layout, so scrolling skips composition
Both are identical; the lambda is only shorter syntax
The first is better because the lambda version allocates on every frame and can't be skipped
The lambda version caches the first offset, so the image never moves
questions.explanation: The non-lambda `offset(y = ...)` reads state during composition, so every scroll pixel recomposes the caller. `Modifier.offset { }` defers the read to the layout phase, so only layout and draw run again.

questions.question: Reading an animated value inside `Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = fade.value }` lets each animation frame skip composition and layout and only redraw.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The `graphicsLayer { }` lambda runs in the draw phase, so state read there only invalidates the layer. `Modifier.alpha(fade.value)` would read in composition and recompose every frame.

questions.question: What does `contentType` give you in this list?
options: Compositions are reused only between items of the same type
The list is grouped and sorted by type before items are laid out
It replaces `key`, so keys are no longer needed
Items of the same type are never recomposed again
questions.explanation: Like view types in a `RecyclerView` adapter, `contentType` lets the lazy list reuse a scrolled-off item's composition for an item with the same structure. It doesn't sort, doesn't replace keys and doesn't stop recomposition.

questions.question: You enable Compose compiler reports and metrics (`reportsDestination` / `metricsDestination` in the `composeCompiler { }` block). What can you learn from them?
options: Whether each class is inferred stable or unstable
Whether each composable is restartable and skippable, with each parameter marked stable or unstable
Module-wide counts such as how many composables are skippable
How many times each composable recomposed on the device
Frame durations and jank while scrolling
questions.explanation: The reports are produced at compile time, so they describe stability and skippability inferred from the code. Runtime numbers like recomposition counts come from Layout Inspector, and frame timing from tools like Macrobenchmark.

questions.question: Strong skipping is disabled in this module, and the compiler report shows `unstable val items: List<Article>` (where `Article` is stable). Which change makes the parameter stable?
options: Change the type to `ImmutableList<Article>`
Change the type to `MutableList<Article>`
Change the type to `ArrayList<Article>`
Change the type to `Array<Article>`
questions.explanation: The compiler knows `ImmutableList` (from `kotlinx.collections.immutable`) can't change, so it treats it as stable. `MutableList`, `ArrayList` and arrays are all mutable, so they're even less stable than the read-only `List` interface.

questions.question: `Screen` recomposes on every scroll pixel only because it reads `scroll.value`. What's the best fix?
options: Pass `offsetProvider: () -> Int` as `{ scroll.value }` and read it inside `Header`
Pass `remember { scroll.value }` instead
Pass `derivedStateOf { scroll.value }.value` instead, so reads are batched
Annotate `Header` with `@Stable` so Compose skips it on scroll
questions.explanation: Passing a lambda moves the state read out of `Screen` into `Header`, ideally into a `Modifier.offset { }` there, so `Screen` no longer recomposes. `remember` freezes the first value, and `derivedStateOf` doesn't help when the result changes as often as the input.

questions.question: A teammate reports that a `LazyColumn` janks while scrolling. Which steps give you representative performance numbers?
options: Measure a release (non-debuggable) build with R8 enabled
Include a baseline profile so the hot code paths are compiled ahead of time
Run it on a real device rather than judging from the emulator
Measure the debug build, since it has the same performance plus extra logging
Keep Layout Inspector's live recomposition counts attached while recording timing
questions.explanation: Debug builds run much slower (the debuggable flag turns off many ART optimizations and there is no R8), so they exaggerate jank. Baseline profiles let critical code be AOT-compiled, and attached inspection tools add their own overhead to timing.

questions.question: With strong skipping on, if the ViewModel emits `items.toList()` with exactly the same contents, `ArticleList(items)` (taking an unstable `List<Article>`) is skipped.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Strong skipping compares unstable parameters by instance (`===`), not `equals()`. `toList()` creates a new instance, so the composable recomposes even though the contents are equal.

questions.question: What happens when this composable runs?
options: It recomposes endlessly, because it writes `count` after reading it
It shows `Count: 0` once and then stops
It shows `Count: 1`, because the write happens before the frame is drawn
It fails to compile, because state can't be written in a composable body
questions.explanation: This is a backwards write: `count` is read by `Text`, then written, which invalidates the composition that just read it, so it recomposes forever. Write state only from event callbacks or effects, never in the composable body.

questions.question: Strong skipping mode is on by default in current versions of the Compose compiler. Which statements about it are true?
options: Composables with unstable parameters become skippable, and those parameters are compared with `===`
Stable parameters are still compared with `equals()`
Lambdas inside composables are remembered automatically, keyed on what they capture
Unstable parameters are compared with `equals()` instead of `===`
Mutating a `var` property of the same instance and passing it again forces the child to recompose
It has to be turned on by hand in every module
questions.explanation: Strong skipping makes every restartable composable skippable: unstable params use instance equality, and stable ones keep using `equals()`. Mutating the same instance still passes `===`, so the child is skipped and shows stale data, which is why immutable models still matter.

questions.question: After a sync bug, two items in `messages` have the same `id`, and they sit next to each other in the list. What happens when that part of the list is shown?
options: It crashes at runtime because the key was already used
The second item is silently dropped
Both items show, but they share the same remembered state
The list falls back to position-based keys
questions.explanation: Keys in a lazy layout must be unique, and a duplicate throws at runtime instead of being merged or ignored. Use a truly unique identifier, such as a database primary key.
